happened: In February 2025, the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) removed all of its NEPA environmental review regulations, effective April 11, 2025, and made the removal final on January 8, 2026. Major agencies, including Interior, Energy, Defense, Transportation and Agriculture, published their own new NEPA procedures in early July 2025. CEQ's guidance tells agencies to focus on an action's direct effects.

key_dates.event: CEQ issues an interim final rule removing its NEPA regulations (effective April 11, 2025).
Supreme Court decides Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, narrowing NEPA review.
Several departments publish new NEPA procedures.
CEQ final rule makes the removal permanent.

legal: In Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County (May 29, 2025), the Supreme Court said courts must give agencies substantial deference on NEPA reviews and that NEPA does not require studying separate upstream or downstream projects. No court ruling blocking CEQ's removal of its rules was found.
closeness: Partial: instead of rewriting its rules like the 2020 version, CEQ removed them entirely and left procedures to each agency. No rule formally bans cumulative impact analysis, but CEQ guidance points agencies to direct effects and notes that NEPA's text does not use the term "cumulative effects."
uncertain: What each agency's new procedures say about cumulative effects was not checked one by one. The Harvard tracker lists no lawsuit against the removal or the agency procedures. Newest source is from June 2026.

happened: CEQ removed its NEPA rules in 2025 (see ch02-044) instead of writing new ones that limit court review. On May 29, 2025, the Supreme Court ruled in Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County that courts must give agencies substantial deference on NEPA reviews. A Trump order also told officials to recommend ways for Congress to streamline court review.

key_dates.event: Supreme Court decides Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County.
CEQ guidance cites Seven County and tells agencies to focus on direct effects.

legal: Supreme Court, Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County (May 29, 2025): courts must give agencies substantial deference in reviewing NEPA documents.
closeness: Court review of NEPA analyses was narrowed, but mainly by a Supreme Court ruling, not by new NEPA rules as recommended. Limits on court remedies were not found.
uncertain: Whether Congress will act on court-review changes is not known. Newest source is from June 2026.

happened: On February 14, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14213, creating a National Energy Dominance Council in the Executive Office of the President. The Interior Secretary chairs it and the Energy Secretary is vice chair. It advises the President on energy production and permitting.

key_dates.event: EO 14213 establishes the National Energy Dominance Council.

closeness: A White House body now coordinates energy policy, but it is a council led by Cabinet secretaries, not a Senior Advisor reporting to the Chief of Staff. It focuses on energy more than environment.
uncertain: How the council coordinates with CEQ and other White House offices in practice is not public.

happened: On January 20, 2025, Executive Order 14148 revoked Executive Order 14008 (Tackling the Climate Crisis at Home and Abroad), the 2021 order that created the White House Office of Domestic Climate Policy.

happened: On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14154. It disbanded the Interagency Working Group on the Social Cost of Greenhouse Gases and withdrew all of its estimates and guidance. On May 5, 2025, OMB, working with the EPA, told agencies to limit greenhouse gas analysis to what their laws plainly require, saying cases needing a dollar value for emissions will be "few to none."

key_dates.event: Executive Order 14154, "Unleashing American Energy," disbands the working group.
OMB memo M-25-27, issued with the EPA, carries out Section 6 of the order.

legal: No court ruling on this part of the order was found.
closeness: Very close: the working group was ended by executive order, and the follow-up guidance tells agencies that dollar estimates of greenhouse gas harm will rarely, if ever, be needed. It is not a total ban: where a law requires an estimate, agencies are to follow the 2003 version of OMB Circular A-4.
uncertain: Whether every agency has stopped using social cost of carbon figures was not checked agency by agency. Newest source is from May 2025.

happened: The President's FY2026 budget proposed moving the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (HIDTA) program to the Justice Department and the Drug-Free Communities program to HHS. Congress did not approve this: the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, signed February 3, 2026, funded both programs at ONDCP. The FY2027 budget proposes the HIDTA move again.

key_dates.event: FY2026 ONDCP budget proposes moving HIDTA to DOJ and Drug-Free Communities to HHS.
FY2026 funding law keeps both programs at ONDCP.
FY2027 ONDCP budget repeats the HIDTA transfer proposal.

closeness: The proposal matches the chapter, but Congress has not approved the moves; both programs stayed at ONDCP for FY2026.
uncertain: Congress's response to the FY2027 proposal is not yet known. Newest source is from April 2026.

happened: On August 7, 2025, President Trump signed an order requiring senior political appointees at federal agencies to review funding announcements and discretionary grant awards to make sure they match agency priorities.

key_dates.event: Executive order "Improving Oversight of Federal Grantmaking" signed (published August 12, 2025).

legal: Court challenges to this order were not checked.
closeness: Broader: the order applies to grantmaking across the government, not only the drug control office (ONDCP). It puts appointees in charge of grant reviews, which matches the chapter's goal of aligning grants with the President's priorities.
uncertain: No source was found showing how ONDCP itself applied the order to its grants. An October 2026 web search found no lawsuit aimed directly at this order, though many grant cuts under earlier orders were challenged. Newest source is from August 2025.
